brief:
Review explanation

K-means with two centroids: how the starting points shape the groups

interactive
Let me move two starting centroids and step through assigning points and updating the centroids. Use a small example where different starts can lead to different groups.

Presentation
Static
Steps
Over time
Experiment

You will see about a dozen points in four small clumps at the corners of a rectangle, plus two marked starting centroids, and the total squared distance from each point to its centroid. Set where each centroid starts with the two position controls for each one. Then press Assign to colour every point by its nearest centroid, and press Update to move each centroid to the average of its points. Keep alternating until nothing changes. Starting the centroids on the left and right gives a different final grouping from starting them at the top and bottom, and the total distance shows which result fits better. Reset puts the centroids back at their starting positions so you can try a new start.

ASSUMPTIONS 2
LIMITATIONS 2

findings.message: These behaviours were not sampled, so I could not judge them: dragging a centroid (drag_start/move/end), a run reaching convergence, and a left/right start that ends in left/right groups. Reading the source, the logic for all three looks correct.
The thin line from B to the right-bottom point at (8.4,1.9) runs straight through the dot at (7.7,1.7). The two lines from A to the left-top points also nearly coincide. You can still read it.

Both starts are set to (10,7), so circle B is drawn exactly on top of circle A. The A label, A's circle and both faint start dots disappear, and the learner can't see or grab A to drag it. Offset or outline centroids that coincide, or add a note when they do.
The assignment line from B to (8.4,1.9) passes through the dot at (7.7,1.7), and the line from A to (8.3,5.1) passes close to the dot at (7.6,4.8). Minor clutter.

Not sampled: dragging a centroid, the left/right versus top/bottom runs to convergence, and the converged message. These cannot be judged from the captures. In the source, a dragged start is not written back to the Start x/y number controls, so the controls can show different values from the start actually used.
The faint line from the left-bottom point to A passes almost through the neighbouring point at about (185,219). This makes it a little unclear which point the line belongs to.

Because A and B start together at the corner (10,7), they are drawn side by side and B's circle extends past the right border of the plot box. A also touches the top edge. The circles should be kept inside the plot area.

manifest.title: K-means with two centroids: how the starting points shape the groups
manifest.summary: Twelve points sit in four clumps at the corners of a rectangle. Drag or set where centroids A and B start, then alternate Assign (each point joins its nearest centroid) and Update (each centroid moves to the average of its points) until nothing changes. Left/right starts give left and right groups; top/bottom starts give top and bottom groups with a larger total squared distance.
assumptions: Two groups and straight-line (Euclidean) distance.
The 12 points are fixed and kept small so each step can be followed.
A point tied between the two centroids goes to A; an empty group keeps its centroid where it is.
Changing a start control or dragging a centroid resets the run to the new starting centroids.
Centroids at the same spot are drawn slightly apart so both stay visible.
manifest.description: A plot with 12 dots in four clumps of three at the corners of a rectangle (left-bottom, right-bottom, left-top, right-top). Two large circles labelled A and B mark the centroids, with faint dots at their starting positions and lines tracing their path. If A and B coincide they are drawn side by side and a note says so. After Assign, every dot is coloured like its nearest centroid and joined to it by a thin line. A side panel lists both centroid coordinates, the number of updates, the total squared distance and a message describing the last step, including when the run has converged.
